inline_text:
A proposal for the Phase 2 theme cards, following the Monitoring & logging card on #9.

**What I can contribute to this repository (CC-BY-4.0, per charter section 9)**

- The row format: Jurisdiction, Instrument and article, Binds, Duty, Scope, Status, Shape defined, plus a "Nothing binding found" list and a revision line.
- Three applicability fields on every row: the role the duty binds (provider, deployer, user, controller, processor), the jurisdiction where it attaches, and the instrument, article and revision.
- The Monitoring & logging card from #9 as the one worked example.
- A sample file in the same format, attached: every requirement row we hold for the 13 binding AI laws on the landscape sheet, 195 rows across the sixteen themes.

**What would stay outside it: the rows for a given deployment**

Which rows apply to a system depends on the parties to each run and where they are, and the rules change often. A register kept in this repository would be a snapshot that goes stale, and picking the rows for a particular system comes close to the "legal advice or compliance solutions" the charter rules out. So the deliverable would say that software reads the rows at run time from a maintained source the deployer chooses. The format is what lets any source plug in.

**One assumption worth making explicit**

The plan so far reads as if each instrument is gathered once: the landscape is a phase that finishes, the extraction prompt runs once per instrument, and September "finalizes" Phase 2. That's a reasonable simplification for a landscape report. It doesn't hold for a register of requirements, and the charter already points the other way ("identify, track, and monitor"). Two rows on the landscape sheet have changed since they were entered:

- Colorado SB 24-205 is listed as effective June 30, 2026. [SB 26-189](https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb26-189), signed 2026-05-14, repealed and re-enacted it as an automated decision-making act that applies from 2027-01-01.
- The EU AI Act row links Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. [Regulation (EU) 2026/1744](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj/eng) amended it from 2026-07-27, in the middle of Phase 2, and moved the high-risk dates to 2027-12-02 (Annex III) and 2028-08-02 (Annex I).

Across the jurisdictions we track, we have recorded at least 71 dated changes to AI law alone (new laws, laws taking effect, amendments, repeals) between 23 April, when the regional owners were named, and today. So a register of AI law is closer to the vulnerability databases than to a survey: it is never finished, and whoever maintains it has to keep re-reading the law. The extraction prompt already asks for each instrument's version, which is the right hook for this.

**The Linux Foundation already splits format from data this way**

- OpenSSF maintains the [OSV schema](https://github.com/ossf/osv-schema). The vulnerability data comes from more than 30 advisory databases run by their own ecosystems (GitHub Security Advisories, PyPI, Go, Rust, Debian and others), aggregated by [osv.dev](https://osv.dev). Tools such as [GUAC](https://github.com/guacsec/guac) (OpenSSF) read those sources at run time.
- [Harbor](https://goharbor.io/docs/main/administration/vulnerability-scanning/pluggable-scanners/) (CNCF) plugs in external scanners, each keeping its own vulnerability database up to date.
- [Open Policy Agent](https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/latest/) (CNCF) separates policy decisions from enforcement; the policies are the user's.
- The other model exists too: the [SPDX License List](https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML) is maintained inside an LF project by the SPDX Legal Team. But it holds license identifiers and texts, and [SPDX](https://spdx.dev/about/overview/) "makes no legal interpretations". Which duty binds which party where is exactly that interpretation.

**A sample in the same format**

[theme-card-sample.csv](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32841505/theme-card-sample.csv)

The attached theme-card-sample.csv is cut from our own corpus ([lexlint.io](https://lexlint.io), disclosure: our site). It holds every requirement row we have for the 13 binding AI laws the landscape sheet already names, from the EU AI Act and Colorado to Vietnam and Korea, in the card's columns plus the start date, the date each text was read and a link to the source. Frameworks and strategies are left out, since they bind no one. The theme IDs are a first pass by wording and obligation class, to be checked when a card is drawn. Vietnam's rows were read at an English translation; the rest link the official publisher.

This is less than I offered on #9, where I said the other fifteen themes would follow as files, each swept like the first. What changed is the licence: anything in this repository is CC-BY-4.0, so whatever goes here is given away on those terms for good. This sample is the part we can give that way. The full dataset isn't, and it seems fair to say why. Today it covers 1,757 laws, about 7,000 obligations and 259 jurisdictions, so the sample is under 3% of it. Each line is read at the law's own text, often in the local language, and re-read when the law changes, which it is doing quickly in 193 of those jurisdictions. Keeping that current is most of the work, and it doesn't stop. (I am also not getting into case law that changes how these written laws are interpreted, usually via judicial decisions, that's a conversation for another day.)

BTW, the trackers in this group's own notes aren't openly licensed either: the [Global AI Regulation Tracker](https://www.techieray.com/GlobalAIRegulationTracker) allows public redistribution only on its commercial plan, the [IAPP Global AI Law and Policy Tracker](https://iapp.org/resources/article/global-ai-legislation-tracker/) is for members, and White & Case's [AI Watch](https://www.whitecase.com/insight-our-thinking/ai-watch-global-regulatory-tracker-united-states) is the firm's own material. The format above doesn't depend on any of them, ours included. If anyone wants to build and maintain an open source of rows, it plugs in the same way. We do allow free usage of our law data, but not under CC BY 4.0.

If the group agrees, I'll open a PR with the format, the worked example and the sample. Happy to take it to Thursday's call.
